slides.title: Measures of central tendency
slides.text:
Measures of central tendency
(Arithmetic) Mean: Also known as the average, is the sum of the values divided by the number of values
Median: The middle value that separates a data set into a higher and a lower half
Mode: It is the value that appears more frequently in a data set

slides.title: Mean
slides.text:
Mean
The mean of a data set is the average of all the data values.
The sample mean X̄ is the point estimator of the population mean μ.

slides.title: Median
slides.text:
Median
The median of a data set is the value in the middle when the data items are arranged in ascending order.
Whenever a data set has extreme values, the median is the preferred measure of central location.
The median is the measure of location most often (Not always) reported for annual income and property value data.
A few extremely large incomes or property values can inflate the mean.

slides.title: Mode
slides.text:
Mode
The mode of a data set is the value that occurs with the greatest frequency.
The greatest frequency can occur at two or more different values.
If the data have exactly two modes, the data are bimodal.
If the data have more than two modes, the data are multimodal.

slides.title: Which Measure to Use?
slides.text: Which Measure to Use?
slides.visual_text: Table of Pros and Cons. Mean: takes all the values into account, sensitive and reliable; biased in presence of extreme values. Median: not affected by extreme values; less sensitive than mean. Mode (the only way to represent nominal data): not affected by extreme values and can be used for qualitative data; it can take multiple values or no value at all, and is less sensitive than mean.

slides.title: Advanced Interpretation: Mean, Median and Mode
slides.text:
Advanced Interpretation: Mean, Median and Mode
When to use? | Strength | Limitation | Example
Mean | Data is symmetric, outliers are absent, and values are all important. | Uses every value, necessary for further analysis (like standard deviation). | Sensitive to outliers. | If the CEO earns ₹10 crore and others average ₹6 lakh, the mean salary could mislead stakeholders.
Median | Data is skewed or contains significant outliers. | Not influenced by extreme values; good for reporting typical outcomes. | Does not use all values in a dataset | Median home price is often used by realtors because it’s not inflated by a few luxury homes.
Mode | Used for categorical data or when identifying the “most popular” is critical. | identifies the most frequently occurring, or “typical,” value in a dataset | May have more than one mode (bimodal/multimodal) or none at all. | Fashion Retail: The most sold t-shirt size (mode) guides inventory purchases. Restaurant Menu: Mode meal ordered helps design new combos.

slides.title: Measures of Variability
slides.text:
Measures of Variability
It is often desirable to consider measures of variability (dispersion), as well as measures of central tendency.
For example, in choosing supplier A or supplier B, we might consider not only the average delivery time for each, but also the variability in delivery time for each.

slides.title: Range
slides.text:
Range
The range of a data set is the difference between the largest and smallest data values.
It is the simplest measure of variability.
It is very sensitive to the smallest and largest data values.
Considers only two values; ignores the rest of the dataset.
Doesn’t tell you how data is distributed between min and max; two very different datasets can have the same range.

slides.visual_text: Left: quartile positions for ungrouped (raw) data: Q1 is the ((n+1)/4)th term, Q2 is the ((n+1)/2)th term (the median), Q3 is the (3(n+1)/4)th term. Right: grouped data formula Qk = L + ((k times n/4 minus F)/f) times h, where Qk is the k-th quartile (k = 1, 2, 3), L is the lower boundary of the quartile class, n is the total frequency, F is the cumulative frequency before the quartile class, f is the frequency of the quartile class and h is the width of the class interval. Bottom: Interquartile Range (IQR) = Q3 - Q1. Purpose of IQR: measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data; useful for identifying outliers and understanding data variability; less affected by extreme values than the range.

slides.title: Interquartile Range
slides.text:
Interquartile Range
The interquartile range of a data set is the difference between the third quartile and the first quartile.
It is the range for the middle 50% of the data.
It overcomes the sensitivity to extreme data values.
Ignores information outside the middle 50%—can overlook important dispersion in the tails.

slides.title: Percentile
slides.text:
Percentile
A percentile provides information about how the data are spread over the interval from the smallest value to the largest value.
The pth percentile of a data set is a value such that at least p per cent of the items take on this value or less, and at least (100 - p) per cent of the items take on this value or more.

slides.title: Percentile Computation
slides.text:
Percentile Computation
Arrange the data in ascending order.
Compute index i , the position of the pth percentile.
i=(p/100) *n
If i is not an integer, round up. The pth percentile is the value in I th position.
If i is an integer. The pth percentile is the average value in i th and i+1 th position.

The average squared deviation of each data point from the mean.

Left table: Name and Weight, with names printed Rishabh (x1), Virat (x2), Rohit (x3), ... and Smriti (xn); below it Mean = x-bar = (x1 + x2 + x3 + ... + xn)/n. slides.title: Variance
slides.text:
Variance
Bessel's correction is a method used in statistics to adjust the formula for sample variance. It involves dividing by n-1 instead of n when calculating these statistics, where n is the sample size. This correction reduces bias in the estimation, particularly when the population mean is unknown and estimated from the sample mean. Statistical resources explain that this adjustment is more accurate, especially when dealing with smaller sample sizes.

slides.title: Standard Deviation
slides.text:
Standard Deviation
The standard deviation of a data set is the positive square root of the variance.
Measures the average distance of data points from the mean.
It is measured in the same units as the data, making it more easily interpreted than the variance.
Limitations:
Still affected by extreme values/outliers.
Assumes distribution is approximately normal for certain interpretations (e.g., "68% within 1 SD").
Not ideal for comparing variability across datasets with widely different means.

slides.title: Coefficient of Variation (CV)
slides.text:
Coefficient of Variation (CV)
The ratio of the standard deviation to the mean, usually expressed as a percentage.
Strengths:
Unitless: enables direct comparison of variability between datasets with different units or means.
Ideal for assessing relative risk or volatility (e.g., in finance, comparing the variability of returns for different investments).
Useful in business for comparing operational processes or production units.
Limitations:
Not meaningful when the mean is zero or very close to zero (can become undefined or misleadingly large).
Less useful if the data contains negative numbers or widely disparate distributions.

slides.title: Coefficient of Variation (CV)
slides.text:
Coefficient of Variation (CV)
In statistical analysis, the coefficient of variation (COV) measures relative event dispersion.
The COV is equal to the ratio between the standard deviation and the mean.
Although COV is most commonly used in comparing relative risk, it may be applied to many types of probability distributions.
CV is arguably a better overall indicator of relative risk when it's used to compare different securities or samples.

slides.title: Practice Problem 2
slides.text:
Practice Problem 2
A company’s HR head is reviewing the monthly salaries (in ₹’000) for employees in the Analytics Department to decide on salary restructuring. There is concern that salary differences within the team may affect motivation and retention.
The monthly salaries (₹’000) of 12 employees are: 42, 45, 48, 50, 50, 52, 55, 58, 60, 62, 65, 95
What does the range indicate about pay disparity in the team?
What does the IQR tell you about the “typical” variation in salaries? Is the majority of employees’ pay clustered or spread?
On average, how much do employee salaries deviate from the mean? Does this number seem large compared to the mean?
Calculate CV% % to compare volatility relative to the average salary. If this department is compared to another with the same mean but a smaller CV, what does that imply?
As the HR head, would you:
Reduce pay disparity to improve fairness and morale?
Or accept it as normal because higher salaries may reflect senior talent?
Discuss how variability measures support your recommendation.

slides.title: Kurtosis
slides.text:
Kurtosis
Peakedness of a distribution
Leptokurtic: high and thin
Mesokurtic: normal in shape
Platykurtic: flat and spread out
Interpreting Kurtosis
Kurtosis ≈ 3 (Excess Kurtosis): Similar to normal distribution (mesokurtic)
Kurtosis > 3: Leptokurtic (heavier tails, sharper peak; more outliers)
Kurtosis < 3: Platykurtic (lighter tails, flatter peak; fewer outliers)

bullets.text: Kurtosis ≈ 3 (Excess Kurtosis): Similar to normal distribution (mesokurtic)
Kurtosis > 3: Leptokurtic (heavier tails, sharper peak; more outliers)
Kurtosis < 3: Platykurtic (lighter tails, flatter peak; fewer outliers)

slides.visual_text: Left: the three shapes. Leptokurtic is a high and thin peak, Mesokurtic is normal in shape, Platykurtic is flat and spread out; drawn as three bell curves of different heights. Right: the formula Kurtosis = (1/n) times the sum from i = 1 to n of ((xi - x-bar)/s) to the power 4, then the interpretation: Kurtosis about 3 is similar to normal (mesokurtic); Kurtosis above 3 is leptokurtic (heavier tails, sharper peak, more outliers); Kurtosis below 3 is platykurtic (lighter tails, flatter peak, fewer outliers).

slides.title: Practice Problem
slides.text:
Practice Problem
A manufacturing company produces electronic components and monitors the thickness (in micrometres) of a critical part. Maintaining consistent thickness is vital to product quality and reducing defect rates.
The thickness measurements (in micrometres) from a sample of 20 components are: 50, 51, 49, 52, 50, 49, 51, 50, 50, 48, 49, 51, 52, 50, 50, 49, 48, 90, 30, 51
Calculate the kurtosis of the sample data.
Interpret the kurtosis value: Does the data display a high peak (leptokurtic) or a flatter distribution (platykurtic) compared to normal? What does this tell you about the frequency of outliers or extreme thickness values?
Would high kurtosis (heavy tails) signal a risk in manufacturing consistency?
What steps might the company take based on this insight? (e.g., tighter process control, equipment calibration, reject limits adjustment).
